variants.title: Run the framework
variants.context: Frame the problem, quantify pressure, draw the smallest path, test failure and trade-offs. Each design decision must trace back to a stated requirement, constraint, or measured risk.
variants.prompt: You are asked to design a ticketing system. Put the interview in order.

items.text: Frame the problem: users, their most important action, what is out of scope, the fact that must stay true.
Quantify pressure: peak reads, writes, payloads, retained data, latency and availability targets.
Draw the smallest path through the source of truth, adding cache, queue, replica, or worker only for a named reason.
Test failure and trade-offs: what the user sees during dependency failure, what can be stale, how it is measured.

variants.hint: The invariant is named before any component.

variants.title: Run the framework
variants.context: Frame the problem, quantify pressure, draw the smallest path, test failure and trade-offs. Each design decision must trace back to a stated requirement, constraint, or measured risk.
variants.prompt: The interviewer changes a requirement halfway through. Put the framework steps you revisit in order.

items.text: Re-state the affected requirement and invariant.
Recompute the pressure the change creates.
Adjust only the parts of the path that the new requirement touches.
Re-test failure behavior and name the new trade-off.

variants.hint: A changed requirement flows through the same order.
variants.explanation: Every decision must trace back to a requirement.

variants.title: Run the framework
variants.context: Frame the problem, quantify pressure, draw the smallest path, test failure and trade-offs. Each design decision must trace back to a stated requirement, constraint, or measured risk.
variants.prompt: You have forty minutes. Put the phases in order with their rough budgets.

items.text: Frame the problem in the first five to ten minutes.
Quantify pressure in the next five to ten.
Draw the smallest path in the next ten to fifteen.
Test failure and trade-offs in the final ten to fifteen.

variants.hint: Time-box the framing so the design gets its share.
variants.explanation: A diagram alone cannot show whether a system is appropriate.

variants.title: State the contract
variants.context: Requirements are observable promises: the functional path, quality targets, the scope boundary, and the invariant that cannot be violated. An assumption is useful only when it changes the design.
variants.prompt: Which of these is an invariant?
options: A confirmed seat is never sold twice.
optionFeedback: The invariant is the fact that cannot be violated.
variants.hint: Which statement must never be false?
variants.explanation: Separate functional path, quality targets, scope, and invariant.

variants.title: State the contract
variants.context: Requirements are observable promises: the functional path, quality targets, the scope boundary, and the invariant that cannot be violated. An assumption is useful only when it changes the design.
variants.prompt: When is an assumption worth stating aloud?
options: When it changes the design; say it and how you would revise the path if it were wrong.
optionFeedback: Assumptions that do not change the design are noise.
variants.hint: Would the design differ if the assumption were false?
variants.explanation: State it: “I will assume 99.9% availability; I will revise if stronger guarantees are needed.”

variants.title: State the contract
variants.context: Requirements are observable promises: the functional path, quality targets, the scope boundary, and the invariant that cannot be violated. An assumption is useful only when it changes the design.
variants.prompt: The interviewer asks about full-text search in a payments design. What is the right move?
options: Name it as out of scope for this answer and explain why.
optionFeedback: A scope boundary is part of the contract.
variants.hint: Which list does this feature belong to?

variants.title: Estimate the pressure
variants.context: Scale estimates are directional: find average demand, multiply by a peak factor, and calculate retained writes separately from reads.
variants.prompt: A service handles 864 million reads per day. What is the average reads per second?

mistakes.feedback: Divide by seconds in a day, not hours.

variants.title: Estimate the pressure
variants.context: Scale estimates are directional: find average demand, multiply by a peak factor, and calculate retained writes separately from reads.
variants.prompt: Average reads are 10,000 per second and the peak factor is 3. What peak rate should the design absorb?
variants.hint: Multiply average by the peak factor.

variants.title: Estimate the pressure
variants.context: Scale estimates are directional: find average demand, multiply by a peak factor, and calculate retained writes separately from reads.
variants.prompt: 20 million writes per day each retain 500 bytes. How many GB are retained per day?
variants.explanation: 20,000,000 × 500 bytes = 10,000,000,000 bytes = 10 GB per day, before indexes and replication.

mistakes.feedback: Twenty million times 500 bytes is ten billion bytes.

variants.title: Explain the boundary
variants.context: Explain each boundary: what a cache may serve stale and how it is invalidated; commit user-visible state before enqueueing side effects; which read must observe a completed write; what the user sees when a dependency is unavailable.
variants.prompt: You add a cache to the read path. What must you say about it?
options: What may be served stale, how it is invalidated or expires, and the behavior on a miss or outage.
optionFeedback: The cache boundary is a correctness statement.
variants.hint: What promise does the cache change?
variants.explanation: Cache safe, repeatable reads; it does not replace the authoritative record.

variants.title: Explain the boundary
variants.context: Explain each boundary: what a cache may serve stale and how it is invalidated; commit user-visible state before enqueueing side effects; which read must observe a completed write; what the user sees when a dependency is unavailable.
variants.prompt: An email must be sent after an order is placed. Where does the queue sit?
options: After the committed write: commit user-visible state first, then enqueue with an idempotent consumer and retry policy.
Before the write, to save time.
optionFeedback: Side effects follow the durable state.
Enqueue-first can send email for orders that never commit.
A queue is not the source of truth.
variants.hint: Which happens first: the promise or the side effect?
variants.explanation: Neither cache nor queue replaces the authoritative record.

variants.title: Explain the boundary
variants.context: Explain each boundary: what a cache may serve stale and how it is invalidated; commit user-visible state before enqueueing side effects; which read must observe a completed write; what the user sees when a dependency is unavailable.
variants.prompt: The recommendation service is down during checkout. What should the user see?
options: A labeled degraded result or a checkout without recommendations; the invariant path stays intact.
optionFeedback: Degrade the optional path; fail closed only on the invariant.
variants.hint: Is this dependency on the critical path?
variants.explanation: State whether the user is rejected, given a pending result, or served a labeled stale result.

variants.title: Close with operations
variants.context: Close with operations: measure the user contract and the boundaries, recover deliberately, and name the trigger for the next design change. A component without a requirement is operational debt.
variants.prompt: How should an interview answer end?
options: By naming the trigger, the signal, and the response: measurements of the user contract and boundaries, deliberate recovery, and the next design change.
optionFeedback: Operations keep the design truthful after launch.
variants.hint: What keeps the design honest after launch?
variants.explanation: Measure p95/p99, success rate, freshness age, cache and queue health, and replication lag.

variants.title: Close with operations
variants.context: Close with operations: measure the user contract and the boundaries, recover deliberately, and name the trigger for the next design change. A component without a requirement is operational debt.
variants.prompt: A candidate adds a second datastore “for scale” with no requirement behind it. What should they say?
options: Name the operational cost: more failure modes, monitoring, and reconciliation; remove it or justify it.
optionFeedback: A component must earn its place.
variants.hint: Which requirement does this component serve?
variants.explanation: Adding a queue, cache, or datastore without a requirement introduces operational debt.

variants.title: Close with operations
variants.context: Close with operations: measure the user contract and the boundaries, recover deliberately, and name the trigger for the next design change. A component without a requirement is operational debt.
variants.prompt: Which statement is a good “next trigger”?
options: When peak writes exceed one primary’s safe headroom, revisit partitioning.
optionFeedback: A trigger names a measurable condition and the design change it drives.
Vague intent is not a trigger.
A technology is not a trigger.
variants.hint: What condition would force the next change?
variants.explanation: Name the metric that would trigger the next design change.
